title: 2 Rooks VS Queen!
reviewNotes: Three branches, 20 exact positions from complete six-piece board. Source corner/king-tempo ideas retained with independent Qe6 defenses and explicit ...Qg8 queen interpositions before Raxg8#/Rfxg8#. Independent loose Rg8+ comparison loses to ...Kxg8. Do not present representative queen replies as an exhaustive source tree.
transcript: Fools will resign because two rooks are much harder to coordinate than a pawn and a queen, but not the player with the white pieces. Instead, he plays rook to G1, the only move that plays for a win. It is important to notice that if the black king goes to the corner, after the very precise king to B7, there is no way to prevent the white rook from going to A8. The black queen has no safe way of checking the white king, and so no matter what happens on the next move, it's going to be checkmate. So black decides to walk out in the open with king to F8. Now, trying to ladder checkmate this king would actually be a massive mistake. The king starts to walk out, and before you know it, you're going to lose a rook. Instead, white finds a brilliant idea, rook to F1. What? Doesn't this simply transpose to the same position? But no, it doesn't, because [music] now this rook is preventing the king from running out in the open, and so rook to G2 is going to lead to an unstoppable checkmate. After king to C7, a move that puts black in zugzwang. The only way to prevent the checkmate would be for the queen to defend the F8 square, but the queen cannot do that because it's the only piece that can move, and so after it does, this is going to be another checkmate. So the king has to keep walking out, but not to E8, because now this would indeed allow the rook ladder that would lead to a checkmate. Black thinks that he's very smart and plays king [music] to E7. Now, the ladder checkmate is not going to work. The king is going to run down to the corner, and now prevent this last check, allowing the black queen to get just enough time to get back in the game. So is this it? Is black simply out of the woods? Well, not exactly, because white continues to check with the rook on the first rank. And if the [music] king goes back like this, well, now we would end up in that same zugzwang scenario that we looked at. So the king keeps walking out, and white continues to check it. Now again, escaping this way would not work, so the king has to head back and we finally managed to force him back into the corner where it came from. And we're going to be playing this zugzwang leading to a checkmate in just a couple of moves.
